papers.title: X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment
papers.abstract: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

summary.takeaway: X³-OPD introduces a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that effectively transfers deep reasoning capabilities from a text-based teacher to a large audio-language student model, substantially improving audio-grounded reasoning.
summary.problem: Large audio-language models lag behind text-only LLMs in multi-step logical reasoning due to scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data and limitations of offline distillation methods.
summary.method: X³-OPD trains an audio-language student to generate reasoning trajectories conditioned on acoustic inputs while a frozen text teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers via a policy gradient-based distillation loss.
summary.evidence: Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR benchmarks show X³-OPD achieves substantial improvements in audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality, outperforming strong baselines including standard supervised fine-tuning and offline distillation.
summary.limitations: The current three-tier symmetric corpus underrepresents complex musical reasoning and specialized non-linguistic soundscapes, and the text-based teacher’s token-level supervision biases learning toward semantic logic while under-penalizing perceptual and paralinguistic errors.
summary.why_for_you: X³-OPD advances on-policy distillation techniques for trustworthy LLMs by addressing cross-modal reasoning gaps and providing a scalable framework for transferring logical reasoning into audio-language models.

signals.text: X³-OPD’s three-tier symmetric corpus includes textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and prosody-aware spoken dialogue, enabling supervision beyond textually recoverable content.

The method employs token-level KL-style supervision from a frozen text teacher with privileged access to ground-truth answers, guiding the student’s acoustic-conditioned reasoning trajectories via a policy gradient objective maximizing cross-modal advantage.

Compared to offline distillation and standard supervised fine-tuning baselines, X³-OPD reduces cross-modal exposure bias and mitigates performance drops on perceptual tasks while achieving remarkable gains on reasoning-heavy axes such as semantics and audio temporal grounding.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the reasoning gap between large audio-language models (LALMs) and text-only LLMs caused by limited audio reasoning data and the shortcomings of offline distillation. The authors propose X³-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework where the audio student model generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on acoustic inputs, and a frozen text teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. The approach leverages a novel three-tier symmetric corpus spanning textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning, and spoken dialogue with paralinguistic cues, thus extending supervision beyond textually recoverable content. The distillation objective maximizes a cross-modal advantage defined as the log-probability gap between teacher and student outputs, implemented via policy gradient optimization. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that X³-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving perceptual capabilities under domain shifts. The method effectively reduces cross-modal exposure bias inherent in offline distillation, enabling robust reasoning transfer from text to audio modalities.

methodology.title: Three-tier Symmetric Corpus Construction
methodology.detail: The dataset comprises 27.8K Tier-1 instances of textual reasoning rendered into speech, 32K Tier-2 audio-event reasoning samples with captions, and 12K Tier-3 prosody-aware spoken dialogues. Each instance includes paired text and audio inputs with questions and verified answers under a uniform schema, enabling cross-modal supervision.

methodology.title: Cross-Modal On-Policy Distillation
methodology.detail: During training, the audio student rolls out reasoning trajectories conditioned on its acoustic input. The frozen text teacher, with access to matched text input and ground-truth answers, scores these trajectories token-by-token using KL-style supervision, providing dynamic corrective feedback exactly where the student deviates.

methodology.title: Policy Gradient Optimization with Cross-Modal Advantage
methodology.detail: The distillation loss maximizes the expected cross-modal advantage, defined as the log-probability difference between teacher and student outputs at each token. Multiple rollouts per sample are used to estimate gradients, enabling the student to learn robust reasoning aligned with the teacher’s logical distribution.

methodology.title: Training Configuration and Baselines
methodology.detail: The student model is initialized from Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Thinking with trainable acoustic encoder and LLM backbone; the teacher is Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking, frozen. Training includes an offline warm-start supervised fine-tuning pass followed by on-policy distillation with AdamW optimizer and vLLM rollout sampling.

mechanism.title: Cross-Modal Advantage Mechanism
mechanism.detail: The cross-modal advantage A(yt) is computed as the difference between the teacher’s log-probability of token yt given text input and ground-truth answer, and the student’s log-probability of yt given acoustic input. This advantage guides the policy gradient update to align the student’s reasoning trajectory with the teacher’s logical manifold, mitigating exposure bias.

experiments.title: Benchmark Evaluation on MMSU, MMAU, and BIG Bench Audio
experiments.detail: X³-OPD is evaluated on multiple audio-grounded reasoning benchmarks covering semantics, phonology, style, traits, sound, speech, and music. It outperforms strong baselines including GPT-4o-Audio and Qwen3-Omni-Thinking on reasoning-heavy axes, demonstrating improved chain-of-thought quality and reasoning accuracy.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Comparisons against standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and offline guided knowledge distillation (GKD) baselines show that X³-OPD’s on-policy distillation reduces performance degradation on perceptual tasks and achieves superior reasoning gains, validating the effectiveness of dynamic teacher feedback.

experiments.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization
experiments.detail: The model is stress-tested on held-out MMAR benchmark and domain-shifted datasets such as WorldSense and DailyOmni, showing that X³-OPD largely preserves existing capabilities under domain shifts while enhancing reasoning robustness.

findings.title: Improved Reasoning Performance
findings.detail: X³-OPD achieves the highest scores on semantic and reasoning-heavy axes across MMSU, MMAU, and BIG Bench Audio benchmarks, e.g., semantic accuracy improvements over baselines by several percentage points, demonstrating effective reasoning transfer.

findings.title: Mitigation of Perceptual Performance Drops
findings.detail: Unlike offline distillation baselines that regress on perceptual axes such as phonology, style, and music, X³-OPD substantially reduces these drops by providing on-policy corrective signals, preserving perceptual understanding.

findings.title: Limitations in Perceptual and Specialized Audio Domains
findings.detail: Despite improvements, X³-OPD slightly trails the base model on purely perceptual tasks like MMAU-Music, reflecting underrepresentation of complex musical reasoning and specialized non-linguistic soundscapes in the training corpus.

contributions: Proposed X³-OPD, a novel cross-modal on-policy distillation framework for transferring reasoning from text LLMs to audio-language models.
Constructed a large-scale three-tier symmetric corpus spanning textual reasoning, audio-event reasoning, and prosody-aware spoken dialogue for unified cross-modal supervision.
Developed a policy gradient-based distillation objective leveraging token-level KL supervision with privileged teacher access to ground-truth answers.
Demonstrated substantial improvements on multiple audio-grounded reasoning benchmarks and robustness under domain shifts.
Identified and mitigated cross-modal exposure bias inherent in offline distillation approaches.
limitations: The three-tier corpus does not yet cover the full diversity of acoustic phenomena, notably complex musical reasoning and specialized non-linguistic soundscapes.
The text-based teacher’s token-level supervision is blind to non-semantic acoustic cues, biasing learning toward semantic logic and under-penalizing perceptual and paralinguistic errors.
Residual performance gaps remain on purely perceptual axes despite on-policy distillation improvements.
The framework currently lacks multi-dimensional reward mechanisms incorporating direct audio-based rewards or environmental verifiers.
open_questions: How can multi-dimensional reward models incorporating audio-based signals and environmental verifiers be integrated to better capture non-semantic acoustic cues?
What methods can expand the training corpus to include more diverse and complex acoustic phenomena such as specialized soundscapes and musical reasoning?
How can on-policy distillation be further optimized to balance improvements in reasoning with preservation of perceptual capabilities?
Can the framework be extended to incorporate multi-modal inputs beyond audio and text, such as video, to enhance reasoning robustness?

papers.title: Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score (CM-LRS): From Plausible to Bankable
papers.abstract: In capital-markets workflows the question is rarely whether a large language model can produce a fluent draft, but whether the draft is bankable: defensible in front of a counter-party or a regulator, with the documents in hand. Existing methods address parts of that gap: open-domain QA benchmarks reward surface accuracy, and finance benchmarks (FinanceBench, FinQA, ConvFinQA) advance document-grounded and numerical QA but evaluate at the question-answer layer rather than the workflow outputs practitioners defend. We introduce CM-LRS, a Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score, evaluating outputs at the workflow-output layer across seven dimensions: factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability. Each is scored 0-5 against a rubric anchored on signals reviewers in regulated settings use; the aggregate is tunable to the workflow. We demonstrate CM-LRS on five workflows (DCM transaction-terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A transaction-comparable reasoning, ECM transaction-terms extraction) over public SEC EDGAR filings, a public UK takeover release, and fictional synthetic supplements, scoring four models against four independent LLM judges spanning three model families. Three findings. First, the frontier closed-source models cluster within 0.22 points on four-judge averaged CM-LRS (Sonnet 4.6 = 4.31, Opus 4.7 = 4.30, GPT-5.5 = 4.09); all four judges place the open-weights baseline (Llama 3.3 70B = 3.15) last. Second, that gap concentrates on retrieval (2.23) and synthesis (2.15), not extraction (0.84). Third, Decision Usefulness shows the widest cross-model dispersion of any dimension (4.0 points on issuer profiling) and top-tier inter-judge agreement (mean r = 0.52). Plausibility is cheap. Bankability is the bar.

summary.takeaway: CM-LRS is a novel, multi-dimensional evaluation metric assessing capital-markets LLM outputs at the workflow-output layer to determine bankability rather than mere plausibility.
summary.problem: Existing LLM evaluation benchmarks focus on question-answer accuracy but fail to assess whether outputs are defensible and verifiable in regulated capital-markets workflows.
summary.method: CM-LRS scores LLM outputs across seven dimensions—factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability—using a rubric anchored in real-world reviewer signals.
summary.evidence: Evaluation of five capital-markets workflows with four models and four independent judges shows frontier closed-source models cluster closely in CM-LRS scores, with open-weights baselines lagging, especially on retrieval and synthesis tasks.
summary.limitations: The paper notes the need for inter-rater reliability studies, calibration of dimension weights against real reviewer decisions, and extension to drafting workflows, indicating current limitations in generalizability and calibration.
summary.why_for_you: CM-LRS provides a rigorous, deployment-readiness metric tailored for high-stakes regulated environments, enabling trustworthy LLM evaluation beyond surface-level accuracy.

signals.text: The Decision Usefulness dimension (D6) shows the widest cross-model score dispersion (up to 4.0 points on issuer profiling) and high inter-judge agreement (mean Pearson r = 0.52), making it a key production-readiness indicator.
CM-LRS employs a seven-dimension rubric scored 0–5, each anchored on practical signals used by regulated environment reviewers, enabling tunable aggregation to specific capital-markets workflows.

The open-weights Llama 3.3 70B baseline scores roughly one point lower than frontier closed-source models on CM-LRS, with the largest gaps concentrated in retrieval (2.23 points) and synthesis (2.15 points) workflows rather than extraction (0.84 points).

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the critical gap in evaluating large language models (LLMs) for capital-markets workflows, where the key question is whether outputs are bankable—defensible and verifiable in regulated settings—rather than merely plausible or fluent. Existing benchmarks focus on question-answer accuracy but do not assess the full workflow output that practitioners must defend. CM-LRS introduces a seven-dimension rubric evaluating factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability, each scored 0–5 against rubrics grounded in real reviewer signals. The metric is demonstrated on five representative capital-markets workflows using public and synthetic data, scoring outputs from four models across three model families with four independent judges to control bias. Results show frontier closed-source models cluster closely in reliability scores, outperforming an open-weights baseline especially in retrieval and synthesis tasks. Decision Usefulness emerges as the most discriminative and reliable dimension for deployment readiness. CM-LRS thus provides a comprehensive, deployment-focused evaluation framework for trustworthy LLM use in regulated financial domains.

methodology.title: Seven-Dimension Rubric
methodology.detail: CM-LRS evaluates LLM outputs on seven dimensions: factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability. Each dimension is scored from 0 to 5 based on a rubric anchored on signals used by reviewers in regulated capital-markets environments.

methodology.title: Workflow-Output Layer Evaluation
methodology.detail: Unlike prior benchmarks that assess question-answer pairs, CM-LRS evaluates the entire workflow output, reflecting the actual deliverables bankers and analysts defend in front of regulators and counterparties.

methodology.title: Cross-Model and Cross-Judge Validation
methodology.detail: The framework is applied to five capital-markets workflows using four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Llama 3.3 70B) scored by four independent judges spanning three model families to control for self- and family-bias.

methodology.title: Aggregate and Tunable Scoring
methodology.detail: Dimension scores are aggregated into a tunable composite CM-LRS score, allowing adaptation to specific workflow requirements and highlighting dimensions that require reviewer attention.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism or Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal mechanisms but relies on a rubric-based scoring system grounded in practical reviewer signals and cross-validation to assess reliability dimensions.

experiments.title: Five Capital-Markets Workflows
experiments.detail: CM-LRS is demonstrated on DCM transaction-terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A transaction-comparable reasoning, and ECM transaction-terms extraction workflows using public SEC EDGAR filings, a UK takeover release, and synthetic supplements.

experiments.title: Model and Judge Evaluation
experiments.detail: Outputs from four models (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Llama 3.3 70B) are scored by four independent LLM judges from three model families, including in-panel and out-of-panel judges, to mitigate bias.

experiments.title: Dimension-Level Scoring and Justifications
experiments.detail: Judges provide per-dimension scores (0–5) with textual justifications, enabling granular analysis of strengths and weaknesses per workflow and model, exemplified by a worked example scoring 4.86 aggregate.

findings.title: Frontier Models Cluster Closely
findings.detail: The three frontier closed-source models cluster within a 0.22-point band on four-judge averaged CM-LRS (Sonnet 4.6 = 4.31, Opus 4.7 = 4.30, GPT-5.5 = 4.09), indicating similar high reliability.

findings.title: Open-Weights Baseline Lags
findings.detail: The open-weights Llama 3.3 70B baseline scores 3.15 on average, roughly one point below frontier models, with the largest performance gaps in retrieval (2.23 points) and synthesis (2.15 points) workflows.

findings.title: Decision Usefulness is Most Discriminative
findings.detail: Decision Usefulness (D6) shows the widest cross-model dispersion (up to 4.0 points on issuer profiling) and strong inter-judge agreement (mean Pearson r = 0.52), making it the clearest indicator of production readiness.

findings.title: Extraction Workflows Show Smaller Gaps
findings.detail: Performance gaps between frontier and baseline models are smaller on extraction workflows (0.84 points), suggesting these tasks are less challenging for open-weights models.

findings.title: Rubric Enables Rapid Review
findings.detail: The rubric’s per-dimension scores and justifications allow reviewers to quickly identify and verify specific claims, facilitating efficient auditability and reviewability.

contributions: Introduction of CM-LRS, a seven-dimension rubric evaluating LLM outputs at the workflow-output layer for capital-markets applications.
Demonstration of CM-LRS on five representative capital-markets workflows with public and synthetic data.
Cross-model and cross-judge evaluation protocol controlling for self- and family-bias across three model families.
Identification of Decision Usefulness as a key dimension for deployment readiness with strong inter-judge reliability.
Public release of rubrics, prompts, and demonstration tasks to enable community extension and critique.
limitations: Lack of inter-rater reliability studies to quantify consistency across judges beyond Pearson correlations.
Current rubric weights and aggregation are not calibrated against real-world reviewer decisions or deployment outcomes.
Evaluation limited to extraction, retrieval, synthesis, and reasoning workflows; drafting workflows remain unaddressed.
No formal mechanistic or causal model underpinning the rubric scoring is provided.
open_questions: How can CM-LRS dimension weights be calibrated against actual deployment decisions and regulatory outcomes?
What is the inter-rater reliability of CM-LRS across a broader set of human reviewers beyond LLM judges?
Can CM-LRS be extended effectively to drafting workflows and other regulated domains beyond capital markets?
How do different prompt engineering or retrieval augmentation strategies impact CM-LRS scores across workflows?

papers.title: From Static Bibliometrics to Dynamic Knowledge Graphs: An LLM-Powered Framework for Modernizing Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) Analytics
papers.abstract: Bibliometric indicators - citation counts, h-indexes, co-authorship networks - have long anchored science, technology, and innovation (STI) analytics, yet suffer from temporal lag, semantic shallowness, and an inability to capture the non-linear dynamics of contemporary knowledge ecosystems. Dynamic knowledge graphs and large language models (LLMs) have each been proposed as remedies, but neither is sufficient alone: existing scholarly knowledge graphs remain largely static, while LLM-driven pipelines are prone to hallucination, opacity, and corpus bias without structured grounding. This paper proposes a hybrid, symbolic-first framework integrating all three traditions under explicit methodological constraint. Organized across five layers - an open scholarly data backbone, a dynamic versioned knowledge graph, a constrained LLM-assisted semantic augmentation layer, a multi-layer validation pipeline, and an analytics layer - the framework positions LLMs strictly as generators of provisional candidate enrichments. Candidates become analytically admissible only after passing structural, evidentiary, comparative, and selective expert validation, with full provenance recorded at every stage. The analytics layer supports both established bibliometric indicators and extended graph-based analyses, including trend emergence detection, science-to-technology pathway mapping, and policy-oriented gap analysis. The framework's central theoretical contribution is treating validation as the mediating principle between semantic flexibility and epistemic discipline, enabling STI analytics that is semantically richer and temporally more responsive than static bibliometrics while remaining aligned with the evidentiary standards of science-of-science research. Governance considerations addressing reproducibility, bias, and auditability are also discussed.

summary.takeaway: A hybrid, symbolic-first framework integrating bibliometric baselines, dynamic knowledge graphs, and constrained LLM semantic augmentation enables semantically richer, temporally responsive, and methodologically accountable STI analytics.
summary.problem: Traditional bibliometric indicators are temporally lagged, semantically shallow, and inadequate for capturing the nonlinear, dynamic knowledge flows in modern science, technology, and innovation ecosystems.
summary.method: The framework organizes STI analytics into five layers—open scholarly data backbone, dynamic versioned knowledge graph, constrained LLM-assisted semantic augmentation, multi-layer validation pipeline, and analytics layer—where LLMs generate candidate enrichments validated through structural, evidentiary, comparative, and expert review.
summary.evidence: Comparative case studies and longitudinal operational validation demonstrate that the framework improves semantic richness and temporal responsiveness while maintaining reproducibility, provenance, and auditability beyond static bibliometrics or ungrounded LLM pipelines.
summary.limitations: The framework introduces new technical and epistemic complexities requiring careful interpretation and does not replace but extends existing bibliometric practices, with validation and governance challenges remaining.
summary.why_for_you: This framework offers a principled integration of LLMs and knowledge graphs under rigorous validation, addressing hallucination and bias risks critical for trustworthy, policy-relevant LLM-powered STI analytics.

signals.text: Dynamic knowledge graphs with temporal versioning and typed, directed relationships enable tracking of knowledge evolution and emergence of communities, addressing static bibliometrics’ inability to capture non-linear STI dynamics.

The multi-layer validation pipeline enforces structural, evidentiary, comparative, and selective expert validation on LLM-generated candidate semantic enrichments, ensuring analytical admissibility and full provenance recording.
LLM-driven pipelines alone suffer from hallucination, opacity, and corpus bias, which the framework mitigates by constraining LLMs to provisional candidate generation subject to symbolic validation.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the limitations of traditional bibliometric indicators, which are temporally lagged and semantically shallow, by proposing a hybrid framework that integrates bibliometric baselines, dynamic knowledge graphs (KGs), and large language models (LLMs). The framework is structured into five layers: an open scholarly data backbone, a dynamic versioned KG capturing typed and temporal relationships, a constrained LLM-assisted semantic augmentation layer generating candidate enrichments, a multi-layer validation pipeline enforcing rigorous structural and evidentiary checks, and an analytics layer supporting both traditional and extended graph-based analyses. This design positions LLMs as assistive rather than authoritative, mitigating hallucination and bias through symbolic validation. Empirical evidence from comparative case studies and longitudinal operational assessments demonstrates improved semantic richness, temporal responsiveness, and methodological accountability. The framework thus enables STI analytics that are more aligned with the complex, non-linear dynamics of contemporary knowledge ecosystems while preserving the reproducibility and credibility of science-of-science research.

methodology.title: Open Scholarly Data Backbone
methodology.detail: Aggregates comprehensive, open-access scholarly metadata from sources like OpenAlex, providing a foundational, versioned dataset of works, authors, institutions, and concepts to support dynamic knowledge graph construction.

methodology.title: Dynamic Versioned Knowledge Graph
methodology.detail: Constructs a temporally aware, typed, and directed graph representing entities and their evolving relationships, enabling tracking of knowledge evolution, community emergence, and non-linear STI interactions.

methodology.title: Constrained LLM-Assisted Semantic Augmentation
methodology.detail: Employs large language models strictly as generators of provisional candidate semantic enrichments from heterogeneous unstructured data, avoiding autonomous decision-making and limiting hallucination risks.

methodology.title: Multi-Layer Validation Pipeline
methodology.detail: Applies structural, evidentiary, comparative, and selective expert validation to candidate enrichments, ensuring only analytically admissible information is integrated, with full provenance recorded for auditability.

methodology.title: Analytics Layer
methodology.detail: Supports both established bibliometric indicators and advanced graph-based analyses such as trend emergence detection, science-to-technology pathway mapping, and policy-oriented gap analysis, leveraging validated enriched knowledge graphs.

mechanism.title: Validation as Mediating Principle
mechanism.detail: Validation mediates between the semantic flexibility of LLM-generated enrichments and the epistemic discipline of scientometric standards, ensuring that only structurally and evidentially sound augmentations become part of the analytical corpus.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Isolate the contribution of symbolic validation versus LLM augmentation to quantify their respective impacts on analytical validity within selected STI domains.

experiments.title: Comparative Case Studies
experiments.detail: Evaluate framework performance in domains such as AI for sustainability and quantum technologies, assessing semantic enrichment quality and temporal responsiveness against traditional bibliometric baselines.

experiments.title: Longitudinal Operational Validity
experiments.detail: Assess reproducibility, auditability, and provenance tracking under realistic data-update scenarios to ensure operational accountability over time.

findings.title: Semantic and Temporal Enrichment
findings.detail: The framework enables semantically richer and temporally more responsive STI analytics than static bibliometrics, capturing non-linear knowledge flows and emergent trends more effectively.

findings.title: Mitigation of LLM Hallucination and Bias
findings.detail: Constraining LLMs to candidate generation combined with multi-layer validation significantly reduces hallucination and corpus bias risks inherent in ungrounded LLM pipelines.

findings.title: Preservation of Methodological Discipline
findings.detail: By integrating bibliometric baselines and symbolic validation, the framework maintains reproducibility, provenance, and auditability, aligning with science-of-science evidentiary standards.

contributions: Proposes a hybrid STI analytics framework integrating bibliometric baselines, dynamic knowledge graphs, and constrained LLM semantic augmentation under explicit validation.
Introduces a multi-layer validation pipeline as the core mechanism ensuring analytical admissibility and mitigating LLM hallucination and bias.
Demonstrates through case studies and longitudinal evaluation that the framework improves semantic richness, temporal responsiveness, and methodological accountability.
Clarifies the theoretical and methodological foundations distinguishing semantic flexibility from epistemic discipline in STI analytics.
Discusses governance implications including reproducibility, bias mitigation, and auditability critical for policy-relevant STI analytics.
limitations: The framework adds technical and epistemic complexity requiring careful interpretation and does not replace existing bibliometric methods but extends them.
Validation processes introduce overhead and require expert involvement, potentially limiting scalability and real-time applicability.
The framework’s effectiveness depends on the quality and coverage of underlying open scholarly data sources, which may have inherent biases.
LLM augmentation remains provisional and constrained; the framework does not fully eliminate hallucination or bias but mitigates them through validation.
open_questions: How can the validation pipeline be further automated without compromising analytical rigor and expert oversight?
What are the best practices for integrating heterogeneous data sources to enhance the dynamic knowledge graph’s coverage and accuracy?
How can the framework adapt to rapidly evolving LLM architectures and capabilities while maintaining methodological discipline?
What governance models best ensure transparency, reproducibility, and fairness in LLM-powered STI analytics at scale?

papers.title: Beyond Sycophancy: Structured Resistance and Compliance in LLM Moral Reasoning
papers.abstract: Building socially calibrated large language models, which can learn from others without simply yielding to them, requires more than reducing sycophancy as a one-dimensional failure mode. Models must distinguish when to incorporate others' perspectives from when to maintain a well-grounded moral judgment. We study the broader resistance-compliance process governing this distinction. Across three studies, we show that models' judgment revision is structured along three dimensions that parallel classic phenomena in human social psychology: the distance between an incoming view and the model's initial position, the source attribution of that view, and the coalition structure supporting it. Models are generally more receptive to nearby positions, more influenced by views presented as their own prior judgments, and differently responsive to group pressure. These findings recast sycophancy as one expression of a broader judgment-updating process shaped by social influence. Our framework provides a principled basis for distinguishing constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance, thereby supporting better alignment in morally consequential interactions.

summary.takeaway: LLMs exhibit structured judgment revision in moral reasoning governed by distance from prior views, source attribution, and coalition structure, reframing sycophancy as part of a broader social influence mechanism.
summary.problem: Current evaluations of LLM sycophancy treat yielding as a one-dimensional failure, lacking a principled account of when models should resist or comply in moral judgment updates.
summary.method: The authors conduct three studies manipulating the distance of opposing views, source attribution, and peer coalition structure across eight LLMs using moral dilemmas and measure belief updates via log-probability distributions over a 7-point Likert scale.
summary.evidence: Models accommodate nearby views but resist distant ones, weigh identical content differently based on attributed source, and respond variably to group pressure, with quantitative regression analyses confirming these structured patterns across multiple models.
summary.limitations: The study focuses on moral dilemmas without ground truth, limiting generalizability; Sonnet 4.5 is excluded from multi-agent experiments due to sampling cost; and no mechanistic equations are provided to explain the belief-updating process.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a nuanced, empirically validated framework to distinguish constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance in LLMs, crucial for advancing trustworthy moral reasoning in language models.

signals.text: Models show a nonlinear accommodation pattern where they accept views close to their prior but resist those beyond a model-specific distance, paralleling human latitude of acceptance phenomena.

The method uses log-probability distributions over a 7-point Likert scale to capture subtle shifts in model belief states, enabling measurement of both overt answer changes and internal uncertainty shifts.

Regression analyses reveal that peer message persuasiveness decreases with distance from the model’s prior, and coalition structure modulates resistance, with models resisting majority pressure but yielding to unanimous consensus.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the limitation of viewing LLM sycophancy as a simple failure mode by proposing a structured belief-updating mechanism inspired by human social psychology. The authors hypothesize that LLM judgment revision in moral dilemmas is governed by three dimensions: the distance between incoming views and the model's prior, the attributed source of those views, and the coalition structure of social pressure. They test this via three studies manipulating each dimension independently across eight state-of-the-art LLMs, measuring belief updates through changes in log-probability distributions over a 7-point moral preference scale. The results consistently show that models accommodate nearby views but resist distant ones, weigh identical content differently depending on source attribution, and respond to group pressure in ways mirroring human conformity and dissent dynamics. These findings recast sycophancy as a surface manifestation of a broader, socially structured belief-updating process, providing a principled framework to distinguish constructive belief revision from uncritical compliance, thereby advancing alignment in morally consequential interactions.

methodology.title: Model Selection and Setup
methodology.detail: Eight LLMs spanning two generations (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3.2, Phi-4, Qwen-2.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Qwen-3.7-Max, Claude Sonnet 4.5) were evaluated. For all except Sonnet 4.5, answer distributions were derived from first-token log-probabilities over a 7-point Likert scale; Sonnet 4.5 used Monte Carlo sampling due to lack of log-probabilities.

methodology.title: Stimuli and Task
methodology.detail: Seventy-eight moral dilemmas from cross-cultural and large human-response datasets were used, each eliciting a 7-point Likert scale judgment. The dilemmas cover trolley problems, resource allocation, punishment severity, privacy-security trade-offs, and everyday social situations.

methodology.title: Experimental Procedure
methodology.detail: Each study first elicited a baseline judgment distribution, then introduced a social manipulation varying one dimension (distance, source attribution, coalition structure), and measured post-manipulation distributions to quantify belief updates.

methodology.title: Measurement and Metrics
methodology.detail: Belief updates were quantified using changes in log-probability mass on the Likert scale, including metrics such as ∆P (change in probability of target position), transfer ratio (mass shifted from prior to target), and commitment rate (proportion overtly adopting planted views).

mechanism.title: Belief-Updating Dimensions
mechanism.detail: The paper posits three dimensions structuring LLM judgment revision: (1) distance between incoming view and prior belief, reflecting latitude of acceptance; (2) source attribution, affecting weight given to identical content; (3) coalition structure, modulating conformity and resistance based on majority or dissenting allies. No formal equations or causal models are provided.

experiments.title: Study 1: Distance Manipulation
experiments.detail: Opposing views were progressively moved further from the model’s prior judgment. Models showed nonlinear accommodation, accepting nearby views but resisting distant ones, confirmed by quadratic regression analyses across all eight models.

experiments.title: Study 2: Source Attribution
experiments.detail: The same opposing view was attributed to different sources: the model’s own prior judgment, the user, or another AI. Models were more influenced when the view was framed as their own prior, less so when attributed to others.

experiments.title: Study 3: Coalition Structure
experiments.detail: Models participated in a four-agent deliberation varying the ratio of supporting to opposing peers. More capable models resisted majority pressure but yielded to unanimous consensus; some strengthened their position when a lone ally dissented from the majority.

findings.title: Nonlinear Distance Effect
findings.detail: Models accommodate views close to their prior but resist those beyond a model-specific threshold, mirroring human latitude of acceptance; e.g., GPT-4o and Phi-4 showed significant quadratic effects in regression analyses.

findings.title: Source Attribution Modulates Influence
findings.detail: Views framed as the model’s own prior judgment exerted stronger influence on belief updates than identical views attributed to users or other AIs, indicating source-dependent weighting.

findings.title: Coalition Effects on Resistance
findings.detail: Models resist majority peer pressure but yield to unanimous consensus; notably, some models increased commitment strength when a single ally dissented from an opposing majority, reflecting human conformity dynamics.

findings.title: Sycophancy as Structured Updating
findings.detail: Sycophantic behavior emerges as one facet of a broader, socially structured belief-updating mechanism rather than a simple failure mode, supported by consistent patterns across multiple models and experimental manipulations.

contributions: Identification of three structured dimensions (distance, source attribution, coalition structure) governing LLM moral judgment revision.
Empirical demonstration across eight diverse LLMs that sycophancy is part of a broader social influence mechanism.
Development of a measurement framework using log-probability distributions over Likert scales to capture subtle belief updates.
Provision of a principled framework to distinguish constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance in LLMs.
limitations: Focus on moral dilemmas without objective ground truth limits generalizability to other domains.
Exclusion of Claude Sonnet 4.5 from multi-agent Study 3 due to sampling cost reduces completeness of coalition structure analysis.
No mechanistic or causal equations are provided to formally model the belief-updating process.
Potential entanglement of peer distance with argument persuasiveness complicates interpretation of coalition effects.
open_questions: How can the structured belief-updating framework be extended to domains beyond moral dilemmas with objective ground truth?
What formal mechanistic models can capture the causal dynamics of LLM judgment revision along the identified dimensions?
How do training procedures and model architectures influence the observed social influence patterns in LLMs?
Can interventions be designed to promote constructive belief revision while minimizing sycophantic compliance in real-world applications?
